meta.titre: Heat transfer: conduction, convection and radiation

sections.contenu_markdown: At a Bamenda market in the cold season, a woman keeps a pot of soup warm in a thick clay container, and a metal spoon left in a boiling pot burns your fingers while a wooden spoon does not. Hot air from a charcoal fire rises, and the Sun warms the roof of your house although there is nothing but space between them. Heat moves in three different ways: conduction, convection and radiation. The GCE asks you to name the right process, to explain how each works, and to link them to everyday devices such as the vacuum flask.

items: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter place to a colder place.
The particles of matter are always moving; they move faster when the body is hotter.
Most substances expand when heated, so a heated fluid becomes less dense.

sections.titre: Three ways in which heat moves
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Conduction.** Transfer of heat through a **solid** (or slowly through a fluid) with no movement of the material as a whole. Hot particles vibrate more strongly and pass energy to their neighbours. In metals, free electrons carry energy quickly, so metals are good conductors. Wood, plastic, air and wool are poor conductors (good insulators). It cannot take place in a vacuum.

**Convection.** Transfer of heat in **liquids and gases** by the movement of the fluid itself. The heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place. This circulation is a **convection current**. It cannot take place in solids or in a vacuum.

**Radiation.** Transfer of heat by **infrared waves** (electromagnetic waves). It needs no material, travels at the speed of light and is the way heat reaches the Earth from the Sun across space. Dull black surfaces are the best absorbers and best emitters of radiation; shiny white or silver surfaces are the poorest absorbers and emitters, and they reflect radiation best.

| | Conduction | Convection | Radiation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medium needed | solid (best), liquid, gas | liquid or gas | none |
| Movement of matter | none | yes, bulk movement | none |
| Works in a vacuum | no | no | yes |
| Example | spoon in hot soup | water boiling in a pot | warmth of the Sun |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how a flask keeps liquids hot (or cold).
variantes.contenu_markdown: The flask has a double-walled glass bottle with a **vacuum** between the walls, so there is no conduction or convection across the gap. The walls are **silvered** to reflect radiation. The stopper is a poor conductor (plastic or cork), which stops heat loss by conduction and by convection from the top. The same design keeps cold drinks cold, because it also keeps outside heat out.

variantes.nom: Convection currents in nature: sea breeze
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about winds or about where to place a heater or a cooler.
variantes.contenu_markdown: By day, the land heats up faster than the sea. Air over the land is heated and rises, and cooler air from the sea flows in to replace it: a **sea breeze**. At night, the land cools faster than the sea and the flow is reversed: a **land breeze**. In a room, a heater is placed low so that warm air rises through the room, and a cooling unit is placed high so that cool air sinks.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks why water is used in a radiator or asks for the heat gained or lost.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The heat gained or lost is $Q = mc\Delta\theta$, where $c$ is the specific heat capacity. Water has a high value, $c = 4\,200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, so a given mass of water can take in a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature. This is why it is used in car radiators and cooling systems.

sections.enonce_markdown: A cook heats $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water in an aluminium pot over a charcoal stove, raising its temperature from $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $85\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Name the process by which heat travels (a) from the glowing charcoal to the bottom of the pot, (b) through the metal bottom, and (c) through the water. Then find the heat gained by the water. Take $c = 4\,200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

etapes.action: Name the process from the charcoal to the pot.
etapes.justification: Hot gases rise and glowing coals send out infrared waves. The pot bottom is touched by hot air, and receives infrared directly.

etapes.action: Name the process through the metal bottom.
etapes.justification: The bottom is a solid and its particles pass the energy on by vibrations and by free electrons, with no flow of matter.

etapes.action: Name the process in the water.
etapes.justification: Water at the bottom is heated, expands and rises, and cooler, denser water sinks to replace it.

etapes.action: Write the heat formula and substitute.
etapes.justification: The heat gained depends on mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise.
Multiply the three numbers and give the unit in joules.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Heat travels by radiation to the pot, by conduction through the metal and by convection in the water. The water gains $378\,000\ \mathrm{J}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "Heat rises, so a fire warms a room by conduction."
items.pourquoi_faux: It is hot air that rises, by convection. Heat itself flows from hot to cold in any direction. Conduction is the transfer in solids.
items.correction_markdown: Say: warm air is less dense and rises in a convection current.

items.erreur_markdown: "A metal handle feels colder than a wooden handle because it is at a lower temperature."
items.pourquoi_faux: Both are at room temperature. The metal conducts heat away from your hand faster, so it feels colder.
items.correction_markdown: Metals are better conductors than wood, so more heat leaves your hand.

items.erreur_markdown: "Radiation needs air to travel through, as the heat from the Sun needs the atmosphere."
items.pourquoi_faux: Radiation travels through a vacuum. The Sun's heat reaches the Earth across empty space.
items.correction_markdown: Radiation is infrared waves that need no medium.

items.erreur_markdown: "Convection can occur in a solid metal rod because the heat moves along it."
items.pourquoi_faux: Convection needs a fluid whose particles can flow. In a solid, particles vibrate in fixed positions, and heat moves by conduction.
items.correction_markdown: A heated metal rod conducts; liquids and gases convect.

items.erreur_markdown: "A shiny silver pot of hot soup loses heat by radiation faster than a dull black pot."
items.pourquoi_faux: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters as well as the best absorbers; shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers.
items.correction_markdown: The dull black pot loses heat faster. Use dull black for cooking pots that must absorb heat, and shiny silver for flasks and reflectors.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the main process of heat transfer in each case and give a reason: (a) the end of an iron bar becomes hot when the other end is in a fire; (b) warmth is felt on the face from a distant bonfire; (c) water at the top of a pot gets hot when the bottom is heated.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Conduction**: the iron bar is a solid, and the particles and free electrons pass energy along it.

(b) **Radiation**: infrared waves travel through the air without heating it much, and are absorbed by the skin.

(c) **Convection**: the hot water at the bottom expands, becomes less dense and rises, carrying heat upward.

items.enonce_markdown: A kettle contains $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A heater of power $1\,500\ \mathrm{W}$ warms it to $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Take $c = 4\,200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and ignore heat lost. (a) Calculate the heat gained by the water. (b) How long does the heater take?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $Q = mc\Delta\theta = 2.5 \times 4\,200 \times (50 - 20) = 2.5 \times 4\,200 \times 30 = \mathbf{315\,000\ J}$.

(b) Energy $= \text{power} \times \text{time}$, so $t = \dfrac{315\,000}{1\,500} = \mathbf{210\ s}$ (3.5 min).

items.enonce_markdown: Two identical cans each hold $0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. One can has a dull black surface and the other a shiny silver surface. After ten minutes in the same room the water in the black can is at $56\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the water in the silver can is at $68\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Take $c = 4\,200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and ignore the heat capacity of the cans. (a) Which process explains the difference? (b) Calculate the heat lost by the water in each can. (c) How many times more heat does the black can lose?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Radiation** from the outside surface. A dull black surface is a better emitter than a shiny silver one, so the black can loses heat faster.

(b) Black can: $Q = 0.5 \times 4\,200 \times (80 - 56) = 0.5 \times 4\,200 \times 24 = \mathbf{50\,400\ J}$. Silver can: $Q = 0.5 \times 4\,200 \times (80 - 68) = 0.5 \times 4\,200 \times 12 = \mathbf{25\,200\ J}$.

(c) $\dfrac{50\,400}{25\,200} = \mathbf{2}$, so the black can loses **twice** as much heat in the same time.

items_markdown: Conduction passes heat through solids by vibrating particles and free electrons; metals are good conductors, air and wood are insulators.
Convection is the bulk movement of a heated liquid or gas: it expands, rises, and cooler fluid sinks to replace it.
Radiation is infrared waves that need no medium; dull black surfaces absorb and emit best, shiny surfaces worst.
A vacuum flask stops conduction and convection with a vacuum and reflects radiation with silvered walls.
Heat gained or lost is $Q = mc\Delta\theta$; water has a high specific heat capacity, $4\,200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
